title: SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip
subtitle: Answer real business questions with SQL: filter, summarise, join and rank a shop's sales data in DataGrip, then export the results to share.
outcomes: Connect DataGrip to a SQLite database and build it from a SQL script
Filter and sort rows with SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY, and handle missing values correctly
Summarise data with aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING, and export the results
Combine tables with inner and outer joins without double counting
Break hard questions into steps with subqueries and common table expressions
Rank rows and work out running totals and monthly changes with window functions
prerequisites: No SQL experience needed: if you've used a spreadsheet, you're ready. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer with DataGrip installed (a free trial is enough, and JetBrains offers free licences in some cases, such as for students). DataGrip downloads the SQLite driver for you.
description: Learn SQL the way data analysts use it: to answer questions. You'll work with the sales data of a small online shop, with customers, products, orders and order items, which you build yourself in DataGrip from a starter script. Each lesson teaches a piece of SQL and then shows it in DataGrip step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux: writing queries with completion, running them, and sorting, filtering and exporting the results. You'll filter and sort rows, summarise them with aggregates and GROUP BY, combine tables with joins without double counting, break hard questions into steps with subqueries and common table expressions, and rank and compare rows with window functions. Every module ends with a lab whose exact results you can check your answers against, and the course ends with a report for the shop's owner, written in SQL and explained in plain language.

modules.title: Connect DataGrip and ask your first questions
modules.summary: Learn how a relational database organises data, build the shop database in DataGrip from a script, and write your first queries with SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.

lessons.title: Tables, keys and SQL
objectives: Describe how a relational database stores data in tables
Explain what primary keys and foreign keys do
Find your way around DataGrip
key_points: A relational database stores data in tables: each row is one thing, such as one customer, and each column is one fact about it, such as their email address.
A primary key is a column whose value identifies exactly one row, such as customer_id; a foreign key, such as orders.customer_id, refers to a row in another table.
SQL describes the result you want rather than the steps to get it: SELECT name FROM products asks for every product's name, and the database works out how to find them.
SQLite keeps a whole database in one ordinary file and needs no server, which makes it ideal for learning; it's built into Python and into many apps.
DataGrip is JetBrains' IDE for databases: it connects to many database systems, completes table and column names as you type, and shows results in a grid you can sort, filter and export.

steps.do: Open DataGrip. On the left is the Database Explorer (called Database in older versions), where your connections, called data sources, appear.
Open Search Everywhere. It finds files, database objects, actions and settings from one box.
Open Find Action and type Reformat Code.
steps.see: The action, with its shortcut beside it: Find Action is a good way to learn shortcuts.

steps.do: Open Settings and look under Database, where you choose how queries run and how results are shown.
Open the Files tool window from View | Tool Windows | Files. It shows the folders and SQL files you work with, and Scratches and Consoles, where DataGrip keeps your query consoles.

lessons.title: Build the shop database from a script
objectives: Create a SQLite data source in DataGrip
Run a SQL script that creates tables and fills them with rows
Explore a table's columns and data
key_points: A data source in DataGrip records how to connect to a database; for SQLite that's the path to the database file, and SQLite creates the file if it doesn't exist yet.
CREATE TABLE defines a table's columns, their types and rules such as NOT NULL; INSERT INTO ... VALUES adds rows to it.
The shop database has four tables: customers, products, orders and order_items, where each order item records which product was bought in which order, how many, and at what price.
SQLite has no separate date type: the shop stores dates as text in the form YYYY-MM-DD, which sorts and compares correctly as text.
The starter script begins by dropping the tables, so running it again rebuilds a clean copy of the data whenever you need one.

walkthrough.title: Create a SQLite data source and run the script

steps.do: In the Database Explorer, click + (New) and choose Data Source | SQLite.
In the File field, choose or type a path for a new file named shop.db in your course folder. If DataGrip says driver files are missing, click the link to download them.
Click Test Connection, then OK.
steps.see: Test Connection reports success, and the new data source, named after the file, appears in the Database Explorer.

steps.do: Open shop.sql with File | Open. If the editor's toolbar shows no data source for the file, choose the shop data source there.
Select the whole script (Edit | Select All) and click Execute, the green arrow at the top of the editor. DataGrip runs the selected statements one after another.
Open the Services tool window to see each statement's result.
steps.see: The DROP, CREATE and INSERT statements, each reported without errors.

steps.do: Click Refresh in the Database Explorer's toolbar, then expand the data source, its main schema and tables.
steps.see: customers, order_items, orders and products.

steps.do: Double-click products to open its rows in the data editor, then click the unit_price column's header to sort by price.
steps.see: 17 products; sorted from the dearest, Coffee Grinder at 38.75 comes first.

steps.do: In a SQL file or console, put the caret on a table's name, such as customers, and open Quick Documentation to see its columns.

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
objectives: Choose columns and compute new ones with SELECT
Filter rows with WHERE, including text patterns and missing values
Sort and trim results with ORDER BY, LIMIT and DISTINCT
key_points: SELECT name, unit_price FROM products returns those two columns for every row; AS names a column, as in ROUND(unit_price * 0.9, 2) AS sale_price.

WHERE keeps only the rows where its condition is true. Conditions use comparisons (=, <>, <, >=), BETWEEN, IN ('Books', 'Games') and LIKE, where % matches any run of characters; in SQLite, LIKE ignores case for English letters.
AND is applied before OR, so unit_price < 10 AND category = 'Stationery' OR category = 'Kitchen' also returns every Kitchen product, however dear; brackets or IN make the meaning clear.
NULL means a value is missing. city = NULL is never true, so test for missing values with city IS NULL or city IS NOT NULL.
ORDER BY sorts the result: ASC (the default) or DESC, with later columns breaking ties. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows, and SELECT DISTINCT removes repeated rows.

walkthrough.title: Write and run queries in a query console

steps.do: Open a query console: right-click the shop data source and choose New | Query Console.
Type SELECT * FROM products; then put the caret on the * and open Show Context Actions. Choose the action that expands the column list.
steps.see: The * is replaced by product_id, name, category, unit_price.

steps.do: Write a query with a filter. As you type a column or table name, completion offers it; open it yourself if it hasn't appeared.
steps.code:
SELECT name, category, unit_price
FROM products
WHERE unit_price < 10
  AND category IN ('Stationery', 'Kitchen')
ORDER BY unit_price;

steps.do: Click Execute in the console's toolbar. If DataGrip asks which statement to run, choose the whole query.
steps.see: Five rows, from Washi Tape (3.25) to Enamel Mug (9.25).

steps.do: Comment out the AND line, run the query again to see what the filter was doing, then put the line back.
Reformat the query so each clause starts on its own line.

lab.title: Build the shop database and ask your first questions
lab.goal: Build the shop database in DataGrip from the starter script, check that every table loaded, and answer four questions about customers, products and orders with SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.
setup: DataGrip installed (a free trial is enough)
Download the starter file shop.sql into a folder for this course

steps.do: Create a SQLite data source whose file is a new shop.db in your course folder. Download the driver files if DataGrip asks, then click Test Connection.
Open shop.sql, choose the shop data source for it, select the whole script (Edit | Select All) and click Execute. Then click Refresh in the Database Explorer.
steps.see: Four tables in the main schema: customers, order_items, orders and products.

steps.do: Open a query console on the data source and check that every table loaded.
steps.code:
SELECT 'customers' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM customers
UNION ALL
SELECT 'products', COUNT(*) FROM products
UNION ALL
SELECT 'orders', COUNT(*) FROM orders
UNION ALL
SELECT 'order_items', COUNT(*) FROM order_items;
steps.see: customers 18, products 17, orders 40, order_items 86.

steps.do: Question 1: which customers live in the United Kingdom? Show their first name, last name and city, sorted by last name and then first name.
steps.see: Five rows: Hannah Clarke (Manchester), Daniel Kim (London), Peter Novak (Leeds), Ravi Patel (London) and Sofia Rossi (Leeds).

steps.do: Question 2: which Stationery and Kitchen products cost less than 10? Show name, category and price, cheapest first.
steps.see: Washi Tape 3.25, A5 Notebook 4.5, Tea Infuser 5.75, Gel Pen Set 6.25, Enamel Mug 9.25.

steps.do: Write question 2's filter without IN or brackets, as unit_price < 10 AND category = 'Stationery' OR category = 'Kitchen', run it and work out why two rows were added.
steps.see: Seven rows: Bamboo Board (21.5) and Coffee Grinder (38.75) now appear.

steps.do: Question 3: which customer's city is missing? Try WHERE city = NULL first, then WHERE city IS NULL.
steps.see: No rows at all, then Omar Haddad (Jordan).

steps.do: Question 4: what were the three most recent orders in May 2025 that weren't cancelled? Show order_id, order_date and status.
Reformat each query before you copy it into your submission.

checks.text: Every table loaded with the right number of rows.
The United Kingdom customers are listed in last-name order.
The cheap Stationery and Kitchen products are right, cheapest first.
The extra rows from the AND/OR version are explained: AND is applied before OR.
The missing city is found with IS NULL, not = NULL.
The three most recent May orders that weren't cancelled are right.

lab.submit: Paste each query with its result (select the rows in the result grid and copy them), and a sentence explaining the two extra rows in the AND/OR version.

-- The shop database for SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip.
-- Run the whole script against an empty SQLite database. Running it again resets the data.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS order_items;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS products;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers;

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    last_name   TEXT NOT NULL,
    email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    city        TEXT,
    country     TEXT NOT NULL,
    joined_on   TEXT NOT NULL  -- a date, as YYYY-MM-DD
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name       TEXT NOT NULL,
    category   TEXT NOT NULL,
    unit_price REAL NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (customer_id),
    order_date  TEXT NOT NULL,  -- a date, as YYYY-MM-DD
    status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('delivered', 'shipped', 'cancelled'))
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (order_id),
    product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products (product_id),
    quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    unit_price REAL NOT NULL,  -- the price when the order was placed
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

hints: If the script stops part-way, check that the data source chosen for shop.sql is your SQLite one, then run the whole script again: it drops the tables first.
Text values go in single quotes, as in 'United Kingdom'. In standard SQL, double quotes are for the names of tables and columns.
Dates are text in the form YYYY-MM-DD, so BETWEEN '2025-05-01' AND '2025-05-31' covers May.

modules.title: Summarise data with aggregates and GROUP BY
modules.summary: Turn rows into answers: count, total and average with aggregate functions, group results by category, month or status, filter the groups with HAVING, and export a summary to share.

lessons.title: Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
objectives: Summarise a whole table with aggregate functions
Explain how aggregate functions treat NULLs
Avoid integer division and round results for reports
key_points: An aggregate function turns many rows into one value: COUNT counts them, SUM adds them up, AVG averages them, and MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest.
COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(city) counts only the rows where city isn't NULL, and COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts different values; the shop has 18 customers but only 17 known cities.
SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULLs, so AVG(x) averages only the values that are there.
In SQLite, dividing one whole number by another drops the remainder, so 7 / 2 is 3; write 7 / 2.0, or use AVG, to get 3.5.

SQLite stores decimals as floating-point numbers, so totals can show tiny errors such as 0.30000000000000004; ROUND(x, 2) tidies a result for a report, and many systems store money as whole cents to avoid the problem.

walkthrough.title: Summarise a table in one row

steps.do: In a query console, count the customers, and the customers whose city is known. Click Execute.
steps.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS with_city
FROM customers;

steps.do: Summarise all the order lines at once.
steps.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)                 AS lines,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders,
       SUM(quantity)            AS units,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), 2) AS average_order_value
FROM order_items;
steps.see: 86 lines in 40 orders, 135 units, and an average order value of 40.44.

steps.do: With the caret inside one statement in a console that holds several, use Extend Selection until the whole statement is selected, then click Execute to run just that one.
Duplicate a line and change the copy to compare whole-number and decimal division.
steps.code: SELECT 7 / 2 AS whole, 7 / 2.0 AS exact;

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
objectives: Group rows and summarise each group
Filter groups with HAVING, and rows with WHERE
Group by computed values such as the month of a date
key_points: GROUP BY category gives one result row per category, and each aggregate in SELECT is worked out from that group's rows.
Every column in SELECT should be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. SQLite runs a query that breaks this rule, taking the value from an arbitrary row in each group, but most databases reject it.
WHERE filters rows before they're grouped and HAVING filters groups afterwards, so HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 keeps only the groups with at least two rows.
You can group by an expression: strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) turns 2025-05-17 into 2025-05, so grouping by it gives one row per month.
CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END turns a condition into a number, so its SUM counts the matching rows in each group.
The clauses of a query are applied in this order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, then ORDER BY and LIMIT, which is why ORDER BY can use names given in SELECT.

walkthrough.title: Group, filter and count with CASE

steps.do: Count the customers in each country, most first.
steps.code:
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY customers DESC, country;
steps.see: 10 countries: United Kingdom 5, Ireland 3, Ghana 2, Nigeria 2, then six countries with 1.

steps.do: Add a HAVING clause before ORDER BY to keep only the countries with at least two customers.
steps.code: HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
steps.see: Four rows.

steps.do: Count the orders in each month, and how many of them were cancelled.
steps.code:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
steps.see: May 2025 is the busiest month: 12 orders, 1 of them cancelled.

steps.do: Click a column's header in the result grid to sort the result there, without changing the query.
Reformat the query.

lessons.title: Export and share results
objectives: Export a query's result to CSV and other formats
Copy results in a format others can paste
Keep queries so an analysis can be repeated
key_points: DataGrip exports a result to a file in formats such as CSV, TSV, JSON, Markdown, HTML, Excel or SQL INSERT statements, and the export dialog sets options such as including the column names as a header.
The same formats, called data extractors, decide what copying from the result grid puts on the clipboard, so a result can go straight into a spreadsheet, a message or a document.
CSV (comma-separated values) is plain text that every spreadsheet opens; a value that contains a comma is wrapped in double quotes.
A saved query, with a comment saying what it answers, can be run again when the data changes; an exported file is a snapshot of one moment.
Before sharing a result, leave out personal data, such as customers' email addresses, that its readers don't need.

steps.do: Run the orders-per-month query from the last lesson, so its result is in the grid.
steps.code:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

steps.do: In the toolbar above the result grid, click Export Data.
steps.see: The export dialog, with a list of formats and a preview of the output.

steps.do: Choose CSV, make sure the column header is included, set the output file to orders_by_month.csv in your course folder, and export.
Open orders_by_month.csv with File | Open to check it.
steps.see: A first line naming the columns month, orders and cancelled, then one line per month.

steps.do: To copy instead, choose a format such as Markdown in the format list beside Export Data, select the result's rows and copy them.

modules.title: Combine tables with joins
modules.summary: Answer questions that span tables: join orders to customers and products, find what's missing with outer joins, and avoid the double counting that joins can cause.

lessons.title: Inner joins
objectives: Join two or more tables on matching keys
Use table aliases to keep queries readable
Let DataGrip complete join conditions from foreign keys
key_points: A join combines rows from two tables wherever a condition is true, usually a foreign key matching a primary key: orders JOIN customers ON customers.customer_id = orders.customer_id.
An inner join, written JOIN or INNER JOIN, keeps only the rows that have a match on both sides.
Table aliases shorten queries, as in FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c; when two tables share a column name, such as unit_price, the alias says which one you mean.
Joins chain: orders to order_items to products shows which products were in each order, and WHERE can then filter on any joined table, as in o.status <> 'cancelled'.
DataGrip knows the foreign keys between tables, so after JOIN it can complete the whole ON condition.

steps.do: In a query console, type SELECT * FROM orders AS o JOIN and use completion to choose customers.
steps.see: Completion offers the join with its ON condition, matching c.customer_id to o.customer_id, worked out from the foreign key.

steps.do: Write the full query for one order's lines, joining all four tables, and click Execute.
steps.code:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_date,
       c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer,
       p.name                             AS product,
       oi.quantity,
       oi.quantity * oi.unit_price        AS line_total
FROM orders AS o
         JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
         JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
         JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_id = 27
ORDER BY line_total DESC;
steps.see: Two lines of Amara Okafor's order 27: Puzzle Cube (3, 22.5) and Bread at Home (1, 18.25).

steps.do: Put the caret on the alias c and rename it to cust. DataGrip changes every use of it in the query.
Put the caret on a table's name in the query and go to its declaration.
steps.see: DataGrip shows the table in the Database Explorer, or opens its definition, depending on your settings.

steps.do: Go back to where you were in the console.

lessons.title: Outer joins and missing rows
objectives: Keep unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN
Find rows without a match, such as customers who have never ordered
Count correctly across a left join
key_points: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; where the right table has no match, its columns are NULL.
LEFT JOIN with WHERE right_table.key IS NULL finds the rows that have no match, such as customers who have never placed an order.
With a LEFT JOIN, COUNT(o.order_id) counts only matched rows, so a customer without orders gets 0, while COUNT(*) would count their unmatched row as 1.
A condition on the right-hand table belongs in ON if unmatched rows must stay: putting it in WHERE removes the NULL rows and turns the LEFT JOIN back into an inner join.
SQLite has supported RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN only since version 3.39; a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped does what a RIGHT JOIN does, and works everywhere.

steps.do: Find the customers who have never ordered.
steps.code:
SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name
FROM customers AS c
         LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.last_name;
steps.see: Peter Novak and Grace Owusu.

steps.do: Count every customer's orders, including customers with none.
steps.code:
SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
         LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY orders, c.last_name;
steps.see: Novak and Owusu at the top with 0, then Ana Garcia with 1.

steps.do: Change COUNT(o.order_id) to COUNT(*) and run the query again.
steps.see: Novak and Owusu now show 1: COUNT(*) counted their unmatched rows.

steps.do: Find the products that have never been sold.
steps.code:
SELECT p.name
FROM products AS p
         LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;
steps.see: Coffee Grinder.

steps.do: In the Database Explorer, right-click the orders table and choose Diagrams | Show Diagram (Show Visualization in older versions) to see the tables and the foreign keys that join them.

lessons.title: Join pitfalls: double counting and checking results
objectives: Explain how joining to a table with many matching rows multiplies rows
Count and total correctly after a join
Check a result a second way
key_points: Joining to a table with several matching rows repeats each row once per match: Amara Okafor's 5 orders joined to their order items give 11 rows.
After such a join, COUNT(*) counts the joined rows; COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) counts the orders.

Adding up a value that belongs to the 'one' side, such as a delivery charge per order, after joining to the 'many' side counts it several times; total each table at its own level first, in a subquery or a CTE.
Decide what counts before you total: the shop's revenue should leave out cancelled orders, which needs orders joined to order_items.
Check a result a second way: revenue by category should add up to the revenue of all orders that weren't cancelled.

walkthrough.title: See the double counting, then total correctly

steps.do: Count Amara Okafor's orders two ways after joining orders to order_items.
steps.code:
SELECT c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer,
       COUNT(*)                           AS joined_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)         AS orders
FROM customers AS c
         JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
         JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
steps.see: 11 joined rows, but 5 orders.

steps.do: Total the revenue for each category, leaving out cancelled orders.
steps.code:
SELECT p.category,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items AS oi
         JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
         JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
steps.see: Games 474.75, Books 409.0, Stationery 402.75, Kitchen 205.25.

steps.do: Check it a second way: the revenue of every order that wasn't cancelled, in one total.
steps.code:
SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders AS o
         JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled';
steps.see: 1491.75, the sum of the four category totals.

steps.do: In the total query, comment out the WHERE line and run it again, to see how much the cancelled orders would have added.
steps.see: 1617.75: counting cancelled orders would overstate revenue by 126.0.

modules.title: Subqueries, CTEs and window functions
modules.summary: Break hard questions into steps with subqueries and common table expressions, then rank rows and compute running totals and month-on-month changes with window functions.

lessons.title: Subqueries
objectives: Use a subquery's result inside another query
Filter with IN, EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
Compare rows with an overall value such as an average
key_points: A subquery is a SELECT inside another statement, in brackets. A scalar subquery returns one value, as in WHERE unit_price > (SELECT AVG(unit_price) FROM products).
IN (subquery) tests whether a value is among a subquery's results, such as customers with a cancelled order: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled').
EXISTS (subquery) is true when the subquery returns any row, and NOT EXISTS finds rows without a match, like a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL.
A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query, as in WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id, so it's worked out again for each outer row.
Beware NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL: if any value is NULL, NOT IN matches no rows at all. NOT EXISTS doesn't have this trap.

steps.do: Find the products that cost more than the average product.
steps.code:
SELECT name, unit_price
FROM products
WHERE unit_price > (SELECT AVG(unit_price) FROM products)
ORDER BY unit_price DESC;
steps.see: Six products, from Coffee Grinder (38.75) down to Jigsaw Puzzle (15.75).

steps.do: Select just the subquery's SELECT, without its brackets (Extend Selection helps), and click Execute to check it on its own.
steps.see: One value: 14.352941176470589, the average price.

steps.do: Find the customers who have had an order cancelled.
steps.code:
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id
                      FROM orders
                      WHERE status = 'cancelled')
ORDER BY last_name;
steps.see: Tunde Adebayo, Liam Byrne and Ravi Patel.

steps.do: Find the products that have never been sold, with NOT EXISTS.
steps.code:
SELECT p.name
FROM products AS p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM order_items AS oi
                  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id);
steps.see: Coffee Grinder, the same answer as the LEFT JOIN in module 3.

lessons.title: Common table expressions
objectives: Write a query as named steps with WITH
Use one step's result more than once
Generate rows with a recursive CTE
key_points: A common table expression (CTE) names a query so the rest of the statement can use it like a table: WITH spend AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM spend.
One WITH can define several CTEs, separated by commas, and each can use the ones before it, so a long question reads from top to bottom as steps.
A CTE can be used more than once in a query, such as comparing each customer's spend with (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM spend).
WITH RECURSIVE builds rows step by step from a starting row, such as every month from January to June, so a report can show months that had no sales.
Build a CTE query a step at a time: run the first step's SELECT on its own, check it, then add the next step.

steps.do: Write the first step on its own and run it: each customer's spend, leaving out cancelled orders.
steps.code:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS spent
FROM orders AS o
         JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
steps.see: 16 rows, one for each customer who has ordered.

steps.do: Wrap it in WITH spend AS (...), then use it twice: to list the customers and to work out the average they're compared with.
steps.code:
WITH spend AS (SELECT o.customer_id,
                      SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS spent
               FROM orders AS o
                        JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
               WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
               GROUP BY o.customer_id)
SELECT c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer,
       s.spent
FROM spend AS s
         JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHERE s.spent > (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM spend)
ORDER BY s.spent DESC;
steps.see: Six customers, from Liam Byrne (226.5) to Hannah Clarke (94.0); the average is 93.234375.

steps.do: Generate one row per month with a recursive CTE.
steps.code:
WITH RECURSIVE months(month_start) AS (SELECT '2025-01-01'
                                       UNION ALL
                                       SELECT date(month_start, '+1 month')
                                       FROM months
                                       WHERE month_start < '2025-06-01')
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', month_start) AS month
FROM months;

steps.do: Reformat the query, so each step's columns line up.

lessons.title: Window functions: ranks, running totals and changes
objectives: Explain how a window function differs from GROUP BY
Rank rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
Compute running totals and month-on-month changes with SUM OVER and LAG
key_points: A window function works out a value from a set of rows related to the current row, written with OVER (...), but unlike GROUP BY it keeps every row.

PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups that are handled separately, and ORDER BY inside OVER sets their order: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) numbers products within each category.
ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows different numbers, in no fixed order unless you add a tie-breaker; RANK gives ties the same rank and then skips (10, 10, 12); DENSE_RANK doesn't skip (10, 10, 11).

SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) gives a running total, and LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) fetches the previous row's value, so revenue - LAG(revenue) is the change; the first row's LAG is NULL.
Window functions are worked out after WHERE, so they can't be used in it: compute them in a CTE or subquery, then filter, as in WHERE position = 1.
Window functions need SQLite 3.25 or later; SELECT sqlite_version(); shows the version you're using.

steps.do: Rank customers by spend with all three ranking functions.
steps.code:
WITH spend AS (SELECT o.customer_id,
                      SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS spent
               FROM orders AS o
                        JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
               WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
               GROUP BY o.customer_id)
SELECT c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name                     AS customer,
       s.spent,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY s.spent DESC, c.last_name) AS row_num,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s.spent DESC)                    AS spend_rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s.spent DESC)              AS dense_spend_rank
FROM spend AS s
         JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
ORDER BY row_num;
steps.see: Ana Garcia and Ravi Patel both spent 54.25: ROW_NUMBER gives them 10 and 11 (by last name), RANK gives both 10 and Kofi Mensah 12, DENSE_RANK gives both 10 and Kofi Mensah 11.

steps.do: Work out monthly revenue with a running total and the change from the month before.
steps.code:
WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)  AS month,
                        SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
                 FROM orders AS o
                          JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
                 WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
                 GROUP BY month)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)       AS running_total,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
steps.see: March: 340.25, a running total of 708.75 and up 230.75 on February; April: down 235.25.

steps.do: Find the best-selling product in each category with ROW_NUMBER and PARTITION BY.
steps.code:
WITH product_sales AS (SELECT p.category,
                              p.name,
                              SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
                       FROM order_items AS oi
                                JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
                                JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
                       WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
                       GROUP BY p.product_id),
     ranked AS (SELECT category,
                       name,
                       revenue,
                       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS position
                FROM product_sales)
SELECT category, name, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE position = 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
steps.see: Fountain Pen (220.5), Bread at Home (164.25), Bamboo Board (129.0) and Puzzle Cube (127.5).

steps.do: Check which SQLite version DataGrip's driver uses.
steps.code: SELECT sqlite_version();
steps.see: 3.25 or later.

project.title: Write a sales report for the shop's owner
project.brief: The shop's owner wants to understand the first half of 2025. Using your shop data source in DataGrip, answer the eight questions in the starter file report.sql, writing one query under each question and keeping the question as its comment. Leave cancelled orders out of every revenue figure. Across the file, use at least one inner join, one outer join, one GROUP BY with HAVING, one CTE and one window function, wherever each fits best. Export the results of questions 3 and 7 as CSV files. Then write a summary for the owner, who doesn't know SQL: what sold best, how sales changed from month to month, which customers matter most, and anything that needs attention, such as cancellations, with at least one recommendation the data supports. To check your work: Games brings in 31.8% of revenue, and the cancelled orders were worth 126.0 between them.
deliverables: report.sql, with a commented query under each of the eight questions
category_revenue.csv and monthly_revenue.csv, exported from DataGrip with headers
A summary of 200 to 400 words for the shop's owner, with at least one recommendation

rubric.name: Correct answers
rubric.description: Each query answers its question correctly, leaves cancelled orders out of revenue, and gives results that match the data.

rubric.name: SQL technique
rubric.description: Joins, grouping, CTEs and window functions are used where they fit, with no double counting; queries use clear aliases and consistent formatting.

rubric.name: A file that can be rerun
rubric.description: Each query sits under its question; the whole file runs from top to bottom without errors on a fresh copy of the database.

rubric.name: Exports
rubric.description: Both CSV files have a header line and the right rows.

rubric.name: Summary for the owner
rubric.description: Plain language and accurate numbers, clear findings, and at least one recommendation backed by the data.

project.submit: Paste report.sql, the result of each query, the first three lines of each CSV file, and your summary.

files.content:
-- Shop performance report, January to June 2025.
-- Write one query under each question, and keep the question as its comment.
-- Leave cancelled orders out of every revenue figure. Revenue is quantity * unit_price from order_items.

-- 1. Which three products earned the most revenue, and how much did each earn?


-- 2. How much did the customers in each country spend in total? Highest first.


-- 3. What share of total revenue did each category bring in, as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal place?
--    Export this result as category_revenue.csv.


-- 4. Which customers placed orders in at least three different months?


-- 5. How many days after joining did each customer place their first order (of any status)? Who was quickest?


-- 6. What was the best-selling product, by units, in each month? Decide how to show ties, and say why.


-- 7. How much revenue did each month bring in, with a running total and the change from the month before?
--    Export this result as monthly_revenue.csv.


-- 8. Which orders were cancelled, who placed them, and how much revenue did each one lose?
